preamble.summary: At the final judgment, the righteous stand with great boldness before those who oppressed them. The wicked, seized with terrible fear, confess that they were wrong: the righteous are now numbered among the sons of God. The wicked admit that their own arrogance profited nothing -- their lives passed like a shadow, a ship's wake, a bird's flight. Meanwhile the righteous live forever, and God arms creation itself to fight against the ungodly.
preamble.remarkable: The wicked's confession (vv. 4-13) is one of the most dramatic passages in all wisdom literature -- a full recantation, too late, by those who persecuted the righteous. The military imagery of God arming creation as his weapon (vv. 17-23) directly inspired Paul's 'armor of God' passage in Ephesians 6:13-17.
preamble.friction: The cosmic warfare imagery (vv. 17-23) sits uneasily with the book's earlier emphasis on God as non-violent creator who 'did not make death' (1:13). The tension between God as gentle wisdom-giver and God as warrior is not resolved but held together.
preamble.connections: Isaiah 59:17 (God puts on righteousness as a breastplate); Ephesians 6:13-17 (the armor of God); Job 7:9 (a cloud that vanishes); Isaiah 40:6-8 (grass withers, flower fades); Psalm 1:4 (chaff driven by the wind).

verses.text_latin: Tunc stabunt iusti in magna constantia adversus eos qui se angustiaverunt et qui abstulerunt labores eorum.
verses.rendering: Then the righteous will stand with great boldness before those who afflicted them and made light of their labors.
translator_notes: The eschatological 'then' (tunc) marks the turning point of the entire first section of the book. The courtroom has reversed: the accused now stand as witnesses against their accusers.

key_terms.note: Constantia means firmness, steadfastness, confidence; the righteous no longer cower but stand with composure before their former oppressors.

verses.text_latin: Videntes turbabuntur timore horribili et mirabuntur in subitatione insperatae salutis.
verses.rendering: Seeing this, the wicked will be shaken with terrible fear, and will be amazed at the unexpected salvation of the righteous.
translator_notes: The wicked's astonishment (mirabuntur) mirrors their incomprehension in 4:14-17. What they could not understand in life now confronts them as inescapable reality.

key_terms.note: The salvation is unexpected only from the wicked's perspective; from God's perspective it was planned all along.

verses.text_latin: Dicentes intra se paenitentiam agentes et prae angustia spiritus gementes:
verses.rendering: They will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit:
translator_notes: The wicked's speech that follows (vv. 4-13) is a formal confession, the most extended speech of remorse in the deuterocanonical literature.

key_terms.note: Paenitentia is regret that comes too late; this is not repentance that leads to restoration but recognition that comes after the opportunity for change has passed.

verses.text_latin: Hi sunt quos habuimus aliquando in derisum et in similitudinem improperii.
verses.rendering: 'These are the ones we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach.
translator_notes: The wicked now quote themselves, acknowledging the contempt they expressed in chapter 2. The literary structure creates a devastating self-indictment.

verses.text_latin: Nos insensati vitam illorum aestimabamus insaniam et finem illorum sine honore.
verses.rendering: We, the fools, accounted their life madness and their end without honor.
translator_notes: The self-designation 'we, the fools' (nos insensati) is the exact reversal of chapter 2, where the wicked considered themselves wise and the righteous foolish.

key_terms.note: The wicked now apply to themselves the very label they had attached to the righteous; the irony is complete.

verses.text_latin: Ecce quomodo computati sunt inter filios Dei et inter sanctos sors illorum est.
verses.rendering: See how they are numbered among the sons of God, and their lot is among the holy ones!'
translator_notes: The 'sons of God' (filios Dei) and 'holy ones' (sanctos) language places the righteous in the heavenly court, among the angelic beings of the divine council (cf. Job 1:6, Psalm 89:5-7).

key_terms.note: This echoes the claim in 2:13, 16, 18 where the righteous man called himself God's son; the wicked now confirm that the claim was true.
The righteous have joined the company of angels and saints; their earthly suffering was the price of heavenly citizenship.

verses.text_latin: Ergo erravimus a via veritatis, et iustitiae lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intellegentiae non est ortus nobis.
verses.rendering: 'So we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us.
translator_notes: The three images of darkness (straying from the path, no light, no sunrise) form a crescendo of spiritual blindness.

key_terms.note: The 'way' metaphor for the moral life is ancient (Psalm 1:6, Proverbs 4:18); the wicked confess they took the wrong road.

verses.text_latin: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis et ambulavimus vias difficiles, viam autem Domini ignoravimus.
verses.rendering: We wearied ourselves on the way of wickedness and destruction, and trudged through trackless wastes, but the way of the Lord we did not know.
translator_notes: The irony: the wicked's hedonistic path, which promised ease and pleasure (2:6-9), turns out to have been exhausting and pathless.

verses.text_latin: Quid nobis profuit superbia? Aut divitiarum iactantia quid contulit nobis?
verses.rendering: What good did our arrogance do us? And what profit did our boasted wealth bring us?
translator_notes: The rhetorical questions expect the answer 'nothing.' The wicked's own accounting demonstrates the bankruptcy of their investment.

key_terms.note: Superbia (pride, arrogance) is the root vice in the Augustinian tradition; here the wicked identify it as the source of their ruin.

verses.text_latin: Transierunt omnia illa tamquam umbra et tamquam nuntius percurrens.
verses.rendering: All those things have passed away like a shadow, and like a rumor that runs by.
translator_notes: The series of transience metaphors that follows (vv. 10-13) is one of the most sustained poetic passages in the book. Each image emphasizes the utter absence of lasting trace.

key_terms.note: The shadow image recurs from 2:5; the wicked's own earlier imagery has come true of themselves.

verses.text_latin: Et tamquam navis quae pertransit fluctuantem aquam, cuius cum praeterierit non est vestigium invenire neque semitam carinae illius in fluctibus.
verses.rendering: Like a ship that passes through surging water, whose track cannot be found after it has gone by, nor the path of its keel in the waves.
translator_notes: The ship metaphor is among the most evocative in ancient literature. Water closes behind the ship; no trace of passage remains. The image was widely imitated.

verses.text_latin: Aut tamquam avis quae transvolat in aere, cuius nullum invenitur argumentum itineris, sed tantum sonitus alarum verberans levem ventum, et scindens per vim itineris aerem, commotis alis transvolavit, et post hoc nullum signum invenitur itineris illius.
verses.rendering: Or like a bird that flies through the air, leaving no evidence of its passage -- only the beating of wings striking the light breeze, and cutting through the air by the force of its flight, the bird passes with beating wings, and afterwards no trace of its course can be found.
translator_notes: The extended bird metaphor is the most elaborately developed of the series, with its attention to the physics of flight. The author seems genuinely fascinated by the mechanics of movement through air.

verses.text_latin: Aut tamquam sagitta emissa in locum destinatum, divisus aer continuo in se reclusus est, ut ignoretur transitus illius.
verses.rendering: Or like an arrow shot at a target: the divided air closes back upon itself at once, so that its path is unknown.
translator_notes: The arrow metaphor completes the series: shadow, ship, bird, arrow. Each is faster and more transient than the last. The climax is the arrow, whose path is invisible even as it flies.

verses.text_latin: Sic et nos nati continuo desivimus esse et virtutis quidem nullum signum valuimus ostendere, in malignitate autem nostra consumpti sumus.
verses.rendering: So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to exist, and had no sign of virtue to show, but were consumed in our wickedness.'
translator_notes: The wicked's confession reaches its devastating conclusion: their entire existence was functionally non-existence. They lived without leaving any trace of good.

key_terms.rendered_as: as soon as we were born, ceased to exist
key_terms.note: A harrowing admission: a life without virtue is equivalent to never having lived at all.

verses.text_latin: Quoniam spes impii tamquam lanugo est quae a vento tollitur et tamquam spuma gracilis quae a procella dispergitur et tamquam fumus qui a vento diffusus est et tamquam memoria hospitis unius diei praetereuntis.
verses.rendering: For the hope of the ungodly is like thistledown carried by the wind, and like thin frost scattered by the storm, and like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest who stays but a single day.
translator_notes: Four more transience images in rapid succession. The cumulative effect is overwhelming: nothing of the wicked's life endures.

key_terms.rendered_as: the memory of a guest who stays but a single day
key_terms.note: The most poignant of the images: a traveler who passes through and is immediately forgotten. Cf. Psalm 39:12, 'I am a stranger with you, a guest like all my ancestors.'

verses.text_latin: Iusti autem in perpetuum vivunt et apud Dominum est merces eorum et cogitatio illorum apud Altissimum.
verses.rendering: But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the Most High takes thought for them.
translator_notes: The abrupt transition from the wicked's dissolution to the righteous' eternal life creates maximum contrast. The terse statement 'the righteous live forever' answers every lament in the preceding verses.

key_terms.note: The book's central affirmation: immortality belongs to the righteous, not as a natural property of the soul, but as God's gift.
A title emphasizing God's transcendence and sovereignty; the righteous are cared for by the highest power in existence.

verses.text_latin: Ideo accipient regnum decoris et diadema speciei de manu Domini, quoniam dextera sua teget eos et brachio sancto suo defendet illos.
verses.rendering: Therefore they will receive a glorious kingdom and a beautiful crown from the hand of the Lord, for with his right hand he will shelter them, and with his holy arm he will shield them.
translator_notes: The imagery shifts from courtroom to coronation. The righteous receive not merely acquittal but royal dignity -- kingdom and crown.

key_terms.note: The righteous inherit a kingdom; cf. Matthew 25:34, 'inherit the kingdom prepared for you.'
The diadem is a royal headband, distinct from the laurel wreath of athletic victory; the righteous are crowned as kings.

verses.text_latin: Accipiet armaturam zelus illius et armabit creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum.
verses.rendering: He will take up his zeal as his full armor, and will arm all creation as his weapon against his enemies.
translator_notes: This verse inaugurates the 'divine warrior' passage (vv. 18-23) that directly inspired Ephesians 6:13-17. God does not merely fight for the righteous but enlists the entire cosmos in the battle.

key_terms.note: Armatura is the complete equipment of a soldier; God goes fully armed.
Divine zeal (zelus/qin'ah) is the passionate energy of God's covenant commitment; it is the motive force behind cosmic judgment.

verses.text_latin: Induet pro thorace iustitiam et accipiet pro galea iudicium certum.
verses.rendering: He will put on justice as a breastplate, and wear unerring judgment as a helmet.
translator_notes: Cf. Isaiah 59:17, 'He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head.' The Wisdom author adapts Isaiah's imagery, which Paul will later adapt again.

key_terms.note: The breastplate protects the heart; justice is God's core identity, not an accessory.
The helmet protects the mind; God's judgment is infallible.

verses.text_latin: Sumet scutum inexpugnabile aequitatem.
verses.rendering: He will take up invincible equity as a shield.

key_terms.note: The scutum is the large Roman infantry shield; equity is the defense that cannot be breached.
Aequitas is fairness, even-handedness; distinct from iustitia, it emphasizes impartiality.

verses.text_latin: Acuet autem duram iram in lanceam et pugnabit cum illo orbis terrarum contra insensatos.
verses.rendering: He will sharpen his fierce wrath into a spear, and the whole world will fight with him against the senseless.
translator_notes: The cosmos itself becomes a combatant. This is not merely divine intervention but the rebellion of all created order against those who violated its purposes.

key_terms.note: Creation fights alongside its Creator; the wicked are not merely opposed by God but by the entire fabric of reality.

verses.text_latin: Ibunt directe emissiones fulgurum et tamquam a bene curvato arcu nubium exterminabuntur et ad certum locum insilient.
verses.rendering: Bolts of lightning will fly with true aim, and will leap to their target as from a well-drawn bow of clouds.
translator_notes: Lightning as divine weaponry is common in ancient Near Eastern imagery (cf. Psalm 18:14, Habakkuk 3:11). Here the clouds themselves are the bow from which the lightning is shot.

verses.text_latin: Et a petrosa ira plenae mittentur grandines; excandescet in illos aqua maris, et flumina concurrent duriter.
verses.rendering: And from a catapult, hailstones full of wrath will be hurled; the water of the sea will rage against them, and rivers will overwhelm them without mercy.
translator_notes: The elements themselves join the assault: hail, sea, and rivers. The passage echoes the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 9:22-26), foreshadowing the extended Egypt comparison in chapters 16-19.

key_terms.note: Literally 'stony wrath'; the image is of a siege engine (petrobalista) hurling stones of divine fury.

verses.text_latin: Contra illos stabit spiritus virtutis et tamquam turbo venti dividet illos et ad eremum perducet omnem terram iniquitas illorum et malignitas evertet sedes potentium.
verses.rendering: A mighty blast will rise against them and winnow them like a whirlwind. Lawlessness will lay waste the whole earth, and evildoing will overturn the thrones of the powerful.
translator_notes: The chapter closes with cosmic judgment: the wicked are destroyed by the very forces they thought they controlled. The thrones of the powerful are overturned -- a reversal that recalls Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:4-8) and the Magnificat (Luke 1:52).

key_terms.note: Spiritus here is wind/breath/spirit; virtutis means 'of power.' The divine wind is both natural phenomenon and spiritual force.
The political implications are clear: unjust power will be dismantled. Cf. Luke 1:52, 'He has brought down the powerful from their thrones.'
